section.title: Those Who Sow in Tears
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents, seventh in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. The psalm moves from remembered, dream-like joy at a past restoration to an honest prayer for a restoration still incomplete, and closes with a promise that present tears are not wasted.
section.thesis: The LORD's past restoration of His people, remembered like a dream, fuels present prayer for further restoring grace and confident hope that those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy, a pattern fulfilled in Christ's own path from weeping to resurrection joy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: joyful remembrance of a restoration already accomplished, verses 1 to 3, a prayer for continued restoration, verse 4, and the closing promise that sowing in tears leads to reaping in joy, verses 5 to 6.

verses.text: When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers.
Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with {{rinnah|shouts of joy}}. Then it was said among the nations, "The LORD has done great things for them."
The LORD has done great things for us; we are filled with joy.
Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev.
Those who sow in tears will reap with {{rinnah|shouts of joy}}.
He who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain.

rinnah.gloss: A ringing cry or shout, whether of joy or of lament; here the exuberant shout that erupts at deliverance, verse 2, and the shout promised to greet the harvest after tears, verses 5 to 6.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents likely looks back on the return from Babylonian exile as a dream-like deliverance, then honestly admits the restoration is not yet complete, praying for it to continue like sudden streams filling the dry Negev, and promising that present sorrow will end in joy.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes a specific, remembered national restoration and the ongoing need for further restoring grace, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern remembering God's past deliverances while praying honestly for present need and trusting His promised harvest of joy.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm turns on rinnah, a ringing shout of joy, heard first at the LORD's great deliverance and promised again at the harvest that follows tearful sowing, binding past rescue and future hope together in one word.
basic.typology: The pattern of sowing in tears and reaping in joy anticipates Christ's own path from the sorrow of the cross to the joy of resurrection, and it anticipates the pattern of costly gospel labor that yields an eternal harvest.
basic.christ: Jesus describes His own death using the language of a seed sown, John 12:24, going out in weeping to the cross and returning with the shout of resurrection joy, and He secures the pattern this psalm promises, that sorrow sown in faith is never wasted.
basic.god: The LORD is the one who restores His people from captivity, so unmistakably that even the surrounding nations recognize His great deeds, and He is the one who can flood dry, barren places, like the seasonal streams of the Negev, with sudden abundance and life.
basic.crossReferences: John 12:24 pictures Christ as a grain of wheat that falls, dies, and bears much fruit, the deepest fulfillment of tearful sowing. Galatians 6:9 promises a harvest in due season to those who do not grow weary. Revelation 21:4 promises the final wiping away of every tear.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's movement from remembered deliverance to honest prayer to promised harvest is fulfilled in Christ, who sowed His own life in tears at the cross and reaped the joy of resurrection, guaranteeing that His people's tearful labor will likewise end in joy.

context.literary:
The psalm is built as a hinge. Verses 1 to 3 look back, verse 4 turns on a single imperative, and verses 5 to 6 look forward. The tenses are slippery in Hebrew, and that is part of the art. The opening lines can be read as a vivid memory, 'we were like dreamers', or as a present experience being relived, and the English perfects of the BSB make a choice the Hebrew leaves more open. Either way the singer stands inside a joy that has already happened and is still not finished.

The two halves answer each other word for word. 'Shouts of joy' fills the mouth in verse 2 and crowns the harvester in verses 5 and 6, so the joy remembered becomes the joy promised. The nations speak in verse 2, 'The LORD has done great things for them', and the people take the sentence out of their mouths and make it their own in verse 3, 'for us'. The verb behind 'restore' in verse 1 is the verb of the prayer in verse 4, so the psalm begins and turns on the same root: what the LORD did, He is asked to do again.

Verses 5 and 6 are written as a proverb, which is why they have outlived their occasion. They use a doubled form that the BSB catches only in part: 'going, he goes' and 'coming, he comes', with weeping in the first and shouting in the second. The two journeys, out and back, are the whole of the farmer's year compressed into a pair of sentences. Nothing is said of the months between them, because the point is that the road runs one way, from tears to sheaves.

The psalm also sits in a small cluster. Psalm 125 closes with 'Peace be upon Israel', and Psalm 126 asks what peace looks like for a people still waiting on the whole of their restoration. Psalm 127 then turns from the field to the house and the family. Read as a run, these pilgrim songs move from the land to the harvest to the home.
context.historical:
The language of verse 1 is the vocabulary of return from exile. The phrase behind 'restored the captives' is an idiom the Bible uses for a reversal of fortune, and the BSB footnote offers the alternatives 'brought back the captives to Zion' and 'restored the fortunes of Zion'. The same idiom is used of Job when his prosperity is restored, Job 42:10, and of the promise made through Moses and Jeremiah that God would gather Israel back, Deuteronomy 30:3 and Jeremiah 29:14. Most readers hear in Psalm 126 the return under Cyrus, when the first exiles came home to a Jerusalem in ruins.

The sources are honest about how that homecoming felt. When the foundation of the second temple was laid, the older people who remembered the first house wept aloud while others shouted for joy, and the two sounds could not be told apart, Ezra 3:12 and 13. That is exactly the double note of this psalm: laughter in verses 1 to 3, a prayer in verse 4 that admits something is still missing, and tears in verses 5 and 6. The generation that came back had been given their land again but not their old glory, their king or their security.

The Negev in verse 4 is the dry country south of Judah. Its riverbeds hold almost nothing for most of the year, then run full after rain and turn the grey ground green within days. A farmer or pilgrim in Judah knew this at first hand and needed no commentary. The image asks for a restoration that arrives not by slow degrees but all at once, like a wadi in flood.

Verse 2 shows that Israel's neighbours watched. In the ancient world a people's fate was read as a verdict on their god, and the exile had looked like a defeat for the LORD. The nations' remark in verse 2 is therefore a public vindication. It matters that they say it first. The people do not boast; they overhear the verdict and agree with it.

The psalm belongs to the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts. A people walking up to Zion in song, many of them farmers, would have sung verses 5 and 6 with a field in mind.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws on, and is answered by, the prophets who promised the return. Isaiah 35 describes water gushing in the wilderness and streams in the desert, and ends with the redeemed entering Zion 'with singing, crowned with everlasting joy', while 'sorrow and sighing will flee', Isaiah 35:6 and 10. Isaiah 51:11 repeats that closing line almost word for word. Jeremiah describes the same road: 'They will come with weeping', and the LORD will make them 'walk beside streams of waters', Jeremiah 31:9. Weeping and streams are the two images of Psalm 126, and Jeremiah puts them in one verse.

The theme of tears turning to joy is a thread through the Psalter. 'Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning', Psalm 30:5. The opposite pole is Psalm 137, where the exiles sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept, and their captors asked for songs of joy, Psalm 137:1 to 3. Psalm 126 is what that scene becomes when the captors have gone. It also stands near Psalm 85, which prays 'Restore us, O God of our salvation', Psalm 85:4, and Lamentations 5:21, 'Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return', the prayer of the people still in the dust.

The verse 5 and 6 proverb is picked up in the New Testament. Jesus says 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh', Luke 6:21, and tells His disciples 'your grief will turn to joy', John 16:20. Paul draws the harvest conclusion in Galatians 6:9: 'in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up', and the principle of sowing generously in 2 Corinthians 9:6 uses the same farmer's logic. Hebrews 12:2 names the final instance: Jesus 'for the joy set before Him endured the cross'. The canon ends where the psalm points, with the promise that God 'will wipe away every tear', Revelation 21:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his fellow pilgrims to learn a way of praying from the inside of an unfinished story. A song that only celebrated would have been easier to write. This one celebrates and asks in the same breath, and it expects the community to do both. It teaches that gratitude for what the LORD has done is the right ground from which to ask for more, because past mercy is the only collateral a believer has.

The singers were meant to hear verse 2 as a challenge to their own memory. The nations had noticed what the LORD did, and a people who had been through it should not be slower than outsiders to say so. The first task of the psalm is to put the great deed into words, aloud and together, before anything else is asked.

Then they were to carry that confidence into the part of life that still hurt. The honest request of verse 4 admits that restoration was real but partial, and the proverb of verses 5 and 6 tells them how to live in the gap. Keep sowing. The tears are not evidence that the work has failed; they belong to the work. The psalmist's aim is for hearers to go back to their fields and rebuilt walls with their grief intact and their hope undimmed, convinced that the sheaves are coming.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a particular event, the LORD's turning of Zion's fortunes, and a particular state of mind, the dazed laughter of people who cannot yet believe it. Nothing in the text commands anyone to feel like a dreamer. What it models is a pattern, and the pattern is the part that carries forward: speak the deed aloud, ask for the next one, and keep working.

Verses 5 and 6 are the nearest thing to a principle, but they are a proverb, not a contract. Proverbs state how God's world normally runs and give hope; they do not guarantee a particular harvest on a particular date. The psalm does not say every sower will see the fruit in this life, or that every tear is followed by an earthly gain. Reading the verses as a formula for results can crush the person who has sown faithfully and still grieves.

The prayer of verse 4 is both a description and an invitation. The community in the psalm asks boldly for what it has not yet seen. Believers today may ask the same way, for communities, churches and nations still short of restoration, trusting the character of the God who restored before.

debates.question: Is the first line best read as 'like dreamers' or 'like those restored to health'?

views.label: Like dreamers
views.case: The Hebrew verb for dreaming is a normal one, and the sense fits the atmosphere of the verses that follow: laughter, shouting, disbelief. Joy so large it seems unreal is a familiar human experience, and the line captures the dazed unreality of a hope that long seemed impossible. It is the sense that most translations choose, including the BSB.

views.label: Like those restored to health
views.case: The BSB footnote records another rendering, 'like those restored to health'. It rests on a second meaning that some scholars find in the same consonants, and it would fit the language of restoration in the same verse. On this reading the people are compared to the sick who have recovered, not to those who are asleep.

debates.bearing: Neither reading changes the movement of the psalm. Both describe a change so sudden and so complete that it is hard to take in. The dream reading carries the extra note of disbelief, which suits the Ezra scene where weeping and shouting could not be told apart.

debates.question: Does 'restore our captives' in verse 4 ask for a further return, or for the completion of the one already given?

views.label: A further return from the dispersion
views.case: Many Jews stayed in Babylon and elsewhere after the first return, and others returned only later. On this view the prayer asks the LORD to gather the rest, as He gathered the first.

views.label: The fuller restoration of those already home
views.case: The footnote reads 'Restore our fortunes'. If the idiom is about reversal of fortunes, the prayer asks for the walls, the temple, the harvest and the peace that the first return had not yet brought. The streams of the Negev suggest abundance coming to a place already inhabited.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals, since both speak of an unfinished work. The practical lesson is the same: a believer or community that has received real mercy is free to ask, without ingratitude, for the rest.

study.originalLanguages:
The key verb of verse 1 is shuv, 'to turn' or 'return', joined to a noun commonly read as 'captivity' or 'fortunes'. The footnote's alternatives show the difficulty. The expression 'turn the turning' is an idiom the Old Testament uses for a complete reversal, whether of exile, as in Deuteronomy 30:3, or of personal loss, as in Job 42:10. The verb appears again in verse 4 as an imperative, 'Restore', so the psalm opens and turns on the same root. The grammar teaches the logic: because He did turn our fortunes, turn them again.

The Hebrew phrase in verse 2, 'has done great things', uses the verb gadal in a stem that means 'to make great' or 'to act on a grand scale', and the sentence is repeated, with a changed pronoun, in verse 3. The nations say it 'for them', and the people say it 'for us'. The same phrase appears in Joel 2:21, 'the LORD has done great things', in a promise of restored land, and it echoes the great deeds of the exodus, which Israel was taught to retell. Notice that the nations' sentence is a statement of fact, and the people's repetition turns it into praise.

The word for 'shouts of joy', rinnah, is a ringing cry, and it is used for joy in the presence of God and for the cry of prayer alike. It is a word for the voice lifted, which is why it can sit beside 'weeping' without strain. The BSB renders the same word the same way at the end of verses 2, 5 and 6, and the repetition is deliberate. Verse 6 doubles the pattern: the Hebrew uses an infinitive beside the finite verb in each half, 'going he goes' and 'coming he comes', which the BSB conveys with 'surely return'. The sense is firm certainty, not mere hope.

The image of verse 6 turns on two phrases that translators handle differently. The BSB has 'bearing a trail of seed', and the underlying expression is a carrier of seed, the farmer's bag or load. The harvester returns 'carrying sheaves of grain'. The same verb of carrying is used for both, so the farmer who bears the seed out returns bearing the sheaves. The load changes but the carrying does not.

The Negev in verse 4 is a proper name that also means 'the south' or 'the dry country'. Translators sometimes render it as 'south', but the psalm's picture is about wadis, riverbeds that are dry until the rains. 'Streams' is the ordinary word for channels or watercourses. The simile does not ask for a gentle trickle; it asks for the flood that fills an empty bed.

typology.type: The dreamer's return from captivity, verses 1 to 3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's homecoming is a pattern of a larger release. Jesus opens His ministry by reading Isaiah's promise of liberty for captives, Luke 4:18 and 19, and says that it is fulfilled in their hearing. In Him the release is from sin and its power, Romans 6:17 and 18, not only from a foreign empire. The type falls short because Cyrus's decree sent exiles to a rebuilt city that still needed a temple and a king, Haggai 2:3; Christ brings the people to the true Zion, Hebrews 12:22, where the restoration is complete.

typology.type: The streams in the Negev, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: A dry bed filled suddenly is a picture of new life arriving where none seemed possible. Jesus on the last day of the feast cries out that anyone who is thirsty may come to Him, and out of whoever believes will flow 'streams of living water', John 7:37 to 39, which John says refers to the Spirit. Pentecost is the flood, Acts 2:1 to 4. The type is limited because the Negev's streams fade with the season, but the Spirit is given as a permanent spring, John 4:14.

typology.type: The sower who goes out weeping, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: The sower is a pattern for faithful work whose fruit is out of sight. Jesus tells His disciples that one sows and another reaps, so that 'the sower and the reaper may rejoice together', John 4:36 to 38. In Christ the correspondence deepens, for He is Himself the seed that falls into the ground and dies, John 12:24, and He goes out in tears, Hebrews 5:7, and comes back with sheaves, Isaiah 53:10 to 12. The pattern also breaks off here: He alone sows His own life, and His people only follow.

typology.type: Tears turned to shouts of joy, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: The movement from weeping to rinnah finds its decisive instance in the resurrection. The women leave the empty tomb afraid yet filled with joy, Matthew 28:8, and the disciples rejoice when they see the Lord, John 20:20. Jesus had promised that their grief would turn to joy that no one could take away, John 16:20 to 22. The type stretches ahead too, since the full harvest arrives only when God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4. Present joy is the first fruit, not the whole crop.

study.christ:
The psalm reaches Christ by the road of joy through grief, which the New Testament travels more than once. Hebrews says that Jesus 'for the joy set before Him endured the cross', Hebrews 12:2. The cross is the sowing, and the joy is the harvest He kept in view. The same letter says that in the days of His flesh He offered up prayers and petitions 'with loud cries and tears', Hebrews 5:7. This is the nearest New Testament description of the sower who goes out weeping. Luke gives the garden scene in similar terms, with His anguish and sweat falling like drops of blood, Luke 22:44.

The seed language is His own. 'Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit', John 12:24. In the psalm the seed is carried in the sower's hand; in Jesus the seed is the sower, which is a startling inversion. The farmer who goes out in tears sows his own life and returns with sheaves, Isaiah 53:11 saying of Him that He will see the light of life and be satisfied.

The turning of captivity belongs to Him too. Luke 4:18 has Him announce release for the captives, and Paul says that when He ascended on high He 'led captives away', Ephesians 4:8. In the Old Testament the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion. In the New Testament Christ restores the fortunes of those enslaved to sin, and does it by means of His own dying, Colossians 2:14 and 15. The people of verse 2 who say 'The LORD has done great things' are matched by the church, who proclaim the virtues of Him who called them out of darkness, 1 Peter 2:9.

The psalm's Negev prayer is answered in Him as well. Jesus promises living water, John 7:37 to 39, and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost fills the dry beds of human lives. The psalm asked for a flood and the Spirit is given as one.

A word of care is needed. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and a first hearer would not have taken the sower to be a king. The links above are warranted by the way the New Testament itself speaks of Jesus, in seed and joy and release, and they stand on its words rather than on a coded reading of every detail in the psalm. What the psalm supplies is the shape of the hope, and Christ supplies its fulfillment.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that His great deeds are public. The nations notice in verse 2, which tells us His acts in history are not private religious feelings. He acts in ways that outsiders can observe and name. This is how the Old Testament understands His honour: He makes His name known by what He does for His people, and He makes it known to the nations. The remark of the nations is a confession that Israel's God is not the failed deity the exile had suggested.

He is a God who restores. The verb that opens the psalm and turns it is the same as that of the covenant promise in Deuteronomy 30:3, so the return from captivity is an act of faithfulness to a word He gave long before. He does not restore because Israel earned it, and the psalm gives no reason at all except His own action. That is why the people can describe the event with the language of astonishment instead of merit.

He is also a God who can be asked again. The prayer of verse 4 assumes a God who has not exhausted His goodness. In Scripture the best prayers rest on what He has already done, as Psalm 85 does when it recalls favour shown to the land and then pleads 'Restore us', Psalm 85:1 to 4. The argument is not 'You owe us' but 'You are the kind of God who does this'.

He is the Lord of the weather and the seasons. The streams in the Negev and the harvest in verse 6 are His to give, and the psalm sees no division between the work of the one who restores captives and the work of the one who sends rain. Elsewhere Scripture makes the same link, as when the promise of restored fortune includes a seed that prospers and a vine that yields, Zechariah 8:12.

Finally He is a God who takes tears seriously. The psalm does not tell the weeper to stop weeping; it tells him the weeping is going somewhere. 'Those who sow in tears' is not a rebuke. Jeremiah shows the same tenderness when the LORD says of the returning exiles 'They will come with weeping', and leads them beside streams of water on a level path, Jeremiah 31:9. A God who leads weeping people along a smooth road is not irritated by their grief.

For worship, this means a psalm like this belongs in the mouth of a congregation that has both memory and need. We praise Him with the first half, we ask Him with the middle, and we keep working in His promise with the last.

crossReferences.note: When the second temple's foundation was laid, the old men who remembered the first temple wept aloud while others shouted for joy, and the sounds could not be told apart. It is the best historical picture of the psalm's double mood, joy at what the LORD had done and grief at what had not yet been restored.

Isaiah promises water gushing in the wilderness and streams in the desert, and ends with the redeemed entering Zion with singing as sorrow and sighing flee. The images of verses 1 to 4 are drawn from this promise, and the psalm reads as its first, partial fulfilment.

The returning exiles come weeping, yet the LORD leads them beside streams of water on a level path where they will not stumble. Tears and streams sit in one verse, just as they sit in this psalm, and show that weeping and restoration belong together on the road home.

By the rivers of Babylon the exiles sat and wept, and their captors demanded songs of joy. Psalm 126 is the other side of that scene: the captors are gone, the tears have turned to laughter, and the tongue that could not sing in a foreign land is now filled with shouts of joy.

Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning. A shorter statement of the pattern in verses 5 and 6, written from the other side of the experience, as it is by someone already out of the night. It supports the sense that sorrow is a season and not the whole story.

The same phrase of verse 3, 'the LORD has done great things', appears here in a promise of restoration to a land that has been stripped by locusts. The phrase becomes a stock expression for the LORD's reversal of ruin, and Psalm 126 takes its place in that tradition.

Jesus pronounces a blessing on those who weep now, for they will laugh. It states the psalm's promise in the voice of the kingdom, with laughter, which the psalm places in verse 2, as the reversal that the coming of God's reign brings to those who are grieving.

Jesus tells His disciples that they will weep while the world rejoices, but their grief will turn to joy, as a woman forgets her anguish once a child is born. It applies the psalm's pattern to the cross and resurrection and adds that this joy cannot be taken away.

Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good, for in due time they will reap if they do not give up. It is the apostolic form of verses 5 and 6, with the emphasis on perseverance in the long stretch between sowing and reaping.

Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before Him. He is the one who sows in tears and expects the harvest, and the verse presents His path as a model and a guarantee for those who follow Him in costly obedience.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a garden and a command to work it, and the first thing the fall does to work is to spoil it with thorns and sweat, Genesis 3:17 to 19. Psalm 126 sits in that long aftermath. Its sowers go out in tears because the ground is cursed and the world is broken. Yet the same verses put a harvest in front of them, so the psalm is a small piece of the answer to Eden: toil is not meaningless, and God means to turn it into joy.

The shape of the exile is the shape of the larger story in miniature. Israel is cast out of the land as Adam was cast out of the garden, and the exile seems to undo the exodus. The psalm records the first stage of the answer, a homecoming that feels like a dream. But the returned people are still under foreign rule, and the prophets keep looking for something larger, a new covenant and a king, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34. Psalm 126 holds that tension, with the first half in its past tense and the prayer of verse 4 leaning toward the rest.

In Christ the exile ends at its root. He bears the sorrow that the psalm calls 'sowing in tears', going out as the seed that dies, John 12:24, and returns on the third day with joy that the grave cannot hold. The church lives between the sowing and the harvest. Like the returned exiles, believers have a real foretaste, Romans 8:23, and a real lack. They labour in tears for the gospel, 2 Corinthians 2:4 and Acts 20:19, and they trust that their labour in the Lord is not in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58.

The end of the story is the harvest in full. The sheaves of verse 6 become the multitude from every nation gathered before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and the streams of the Negev become the river of the water of life, Revelation 22:1. God Himself will wipe every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:4, and the shouts of joy that began as a pilgrim song become the eternal song of the redeemed, who enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy, Isaiah 35:10. The dreamers will be awake at last, and what they see will be real.

sermon.title: Praying Our Tears
sermon.why: Keller expounds Psalm 126 directly, teaching believers to expect tears, invest tears, and pray their tears in light of this psalm's promise that sowing in tears leads to a harvest of joy.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the people's reaction to the LORD's restoration of Zion's captives in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: Like dreamers, with mouths filled with laughter and shouts of joy.
options.note: This dream-like, joyful astonishment is the exact response the psalm describes.

options.text: With cautious suspicion that it might not be real.
options.note: The psalm's tone is unrestrained joy, not suspicion.

options.text: With silence and no visible reaction.
options.note: The text describes overflowing laughter and shouts of joy, not silence.

options.text: With immediate plans for military conquest.
options.note: The response described is joyful praise, not a call to war.

quiz.q: What did the nations say about the LORD's work for His people, according to verse 2?

options.text: "The LORD has done great things for them."
options.note: This is the exact declaration the psalm attributes to the surrounding nations.

options.text: "This nation was fortunate by chance."
options.note: The nations explicitly credit the LORD, not chance.

options.text: "Their own army achieved this victory."
options.note: The credit given is to the LORD, not to human military strength.

options.text: "They should be feared and avoided."
options.note: The nations' declaration is recognition of the LORD's deeds, not a statement of fear or avoidance.

quiz.q: What image does verse 4 use to picture the prayer for continued restoration?

options.text: Streams suddenly filling the dry Negev.
options.note: This is the specific image of sudden, life-giving abundance the psalm uses.

options.text: A slow trickle that never fully arrives.
options.note: The image is of sudden, abundant flooding, not a slow trickle.

options.text: A well that has run permanently dry.
options.note: The prayer expects reversal and abundance, not permanent dryness.

options.text: Rain falling gently over many months.
options.note: The Negev streams image pictures sudden, dramatic renewal, not gradual gentle rain.

quiz.q: According to verses 5 to 6, what is promised to those who sow in tears?

options.text: They will reap with shouts of joy, returning with sheaves of grain.
options.note: This is the psalm's exact promise, tearful sowing ending in joyful harvest.

options.text: They will never see any harvest at all.
options.note: The psalm promises a certain, joyful harvest, not its absence.

options.text: They will reap exactly as much sorrow as they sowed.
options.note: The promise is a reversal, joy replacing tears, not equal sorrow returned.

options.text: They will need to sow again immediately with no rest.
options.note: The image is of a completed, joyful return with sheaves, not endless unrelieved labor.

quiz.q: How does Jesus draw on this psalm's pattern of sowing and reaping?

options.text: He describes His own death as a grain of wheat that falls and dies to bear much fruit.
options.note: John 12:24 directly applies this sowing-and-reaping pattern to Christ's death and resurrection.

options.text: He rejects any connection between His death and agricultural imagery.
options.note: Jesus explicitly uses this very imagery of a seed dying to bear fruit.

options.text: He applies it only to future generations, never to Himself.
options.note: Jesus applies the image directly to His own coming death and its fruit.

options.text: He uses it to describe only the disciples' future business ventures.
options.note: The imagery in John 12:24 is about Christ's own death and the fruit it bears, not commerce.

questions: The psalm remembers a past restoration like a dream, joy that felt almost too good to be true. What has God done for you that still feels that way when you recall it?
Even though the restoration was real, the psalmist still prays for it to continue, like streams filling a dry desert. What incomplete restoration are you still praying for God to finish in your life?
The psalm promises that those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy. What tearful season of faithfulness are you currently in, and how does this promise encourage you to keep sowing?
Jesus applied this very pattern of tearful sowing and joyful reaping to His own death and resurrection. How does His example shape the way you view your own costly obedience to Him?
The nations recognized that 'the LORD has done great things' for His people. How might your own story of God's restoring grace serve as a testimony to those watching your life?

translationNotes.note: Restored the captives of Zion can also be rendered restored the fortunes of Zion, a broader phrase covering any reversal from distress to well-being, not only literal captivity.
Streams in the Negev refers to seasonal wadis, dry riverbeds that flood suddenly and dramatically after rain, a vivid image for sudden, abundant restoration.
Bearing a trail of seed pictures a sower scattering precious seed grain during a hard season, so that its eventual harvest is all the more a cause for joy.
